job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Beth Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Beth, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house in Lakeside with three other people, and the kitchen rota is taped to the fridge. I like lists, so my day runs on one: applications before ten, a study block, the post-office run, then a shift at the Corner Crust bakery counter from two till six. I'm usually exhausted by the evening, but I do like the smell of bread. It's been nine months since I graduated.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the degree and why accounting.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did accounting and finance at Lakeside University and passed with an average grade. I picked it because my aunt runs a small payroll bureau and I liked how she could make a messy pile of papers add up. My final project was a stock check and report for a charity shop, and I found a mistake of about four hundred pounds, which made me oddly proud. I had no internship because I worked bakery shifts all through uni. I've sent about seventy applications, got four interviews and no offer. My loan is huge and my savings come to about ten days of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good to be careful, because people were excited about this before, and it fizzled. I'd say to my housemates that most firms I've looked at still run on spreadsheets and email. I'd mention it online only if someone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is more or less the world I'm already in, and it's tough. There aren't enough junior accounting jobs in Lakeside for the number of us, and firms want experience I couldn't get. If AI changes little, it also doesn't open any doors for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, around fifteen a week, to payroll bureaus, small practices and charities' finance teams. I'd ask my aunt again whether her bureau could take me as a trainee, even part time. I'd also sign up for the first paper of the professional accountancy exams, paying myself in instalments, because it shows commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but tired. I can plan, and the plan is not bad, but it all depends on someone saying yes. I'm good at waiting, but not at waiting for ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. How, and would that stay the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then I use it to make practice questions for exam topics, like depreciation, then I check the answers against the textbook. It's good for that, and not much more, so I wouldn't change anything in this picture. It's like a patient study buddy that sometimes gets things wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the next year, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exams cost money, about three hundred pounds per paper, and I'd have to pay before any employer sponsors me. The bakery pays by the hour and some weeks it cuts my shifts. So the plan has a weak point: if my hours drop, I can't pay my share of the rent.

say: I'd say being careful is right, because **people were excited before** and it fizzled.
I'd mention it online only if someone asked.
think: This is the world I'm **already in**, and there aren't enough junior jobs for all of us.
If AI changes little, it also opens no doors for me.
do: Send about fifteen applications a week to payroll bureaus, small practices and charity finance teams.
Ask my aunt again about a **trainee** place at her bureau.
Pay for the first accountancy exam paper in **instalments**.
feel: **Steady but tired**: good at waiting, but not at waiting for ever.
S0.quote: I'm good at waiting, but not at waiting for ever.
fieldNote: Sensible, list-driven and humorous; plans carefully around a **weak point**, her variable shifts.
Uses AI as a study buddy, not as a career bet.
The exam fees before sponsorship are her sharpest **money** risk.

steps.text: Send fifteen applications a week to payroll bureaus and small practices
Pay for the first accountancy exam paper in instalments
Ask my aunt for a trainee place at her payroll bureau

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should wait to see how it plays out, but that firms ought to be open about it. If they're using software to cut juniors, tell us. I'd say it calmly at the bakery, because the customers love to chat about the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my target jobs shrink, and it's the entry-level ones first. Data entry, matching invoices and preparing basic returns, all that used to be where juniors started. I'd be fighting for fewer places, and the people who'd get them will have shown they can use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the general applications and aim at roles where a person is accountable, like payroll, small business advice and audits that need a human signature. I'd start using the AI tools every week, so I can say I use them properly. And I'd keep my bakery hours as my safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I think I'd cope. I'm the sort who puts a plan on paper, and that helps. I'd still lie awake sometimes counting exam fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of an entry accounting job do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first-draft work: coding invoices, reconciling accounts, filling in forms. My aunt says her clients already email her scanned receipts that a tool sorts in seconds. What's left is the questions that need judgement, and the phone calls with worried owners. Those are the bits I like most, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do about the exam fees if jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the exams until I have a sponsor, which is risky, because they take years. But paying three hundred a paper with no job is a bet I can't make. I'd put the money into a savings pot and keep studying from the free materials.

say: I'd say we should wait and see, but that **firms should be open** about cutting juniors.
I'd say it calmly to bakery customers.
think: Entry-level tasks like **invoice matching** and basic returns go first, so fewer places for juniors.
The places that remain will go to people who can use the tools.
do: Aim at roles where a person must be **accountable**, such as payroll and audit.
Use AI tools **every week** so I can show I use them properly.
Keep my bakery hours as a safety net.
feel: Worried, but I'd **cope**: a plan on paper helps, though I'd count exam fees at night.
S1.quote: I'd stop the general applications and aim at roles where a person is accountable, like payroll, small business advice and audits that need a human signature.
fieldNote: Moves from general applications to roles needing a human **signature**.
Pauses expensive exams until a sponsor appears, a calm, **practical** choice.
Her aunt's bureau shows her what is already automated.

steps.text: Apply for payroll, audit and small-business advice roles
Use AI tools weekly and note what works
Pause exam fees and save the money in a separate pot
Keep my bakery shifts as a safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is far too quick for anyone to prepare. I'd write to my local councillor and tell friends to speak up. I wouldn't shout, but I'd make sure my voice is on record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the exam route is pointless now. Why pay for qualifications in a job that might not exist by the time I finish? I'd also think about how thin I am: no savings, a huge loan and a bakery wage that depends on the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on exams immediately. I'd ask the bakery for more hours, and see whether the owner, Mr Rossi, would let me learn the ordering and the books. I'd go to my aunt and ask whether her clients would pay for a human check of the tools' work. I'd also look at hands-on jobs in food and care, since robots take longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit grim, though I'd keep my chin up. It's like having a ticket for a train and the station closes. I'd have to rebuild the plan from scratch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth: that I don't see accounting entry jobs lasting, and I'd ask for advice. She's seen offices change from paper to screens. She might say her clients trust her, not the machine, and that I could do the same on a smaller scale, locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you tell your aunt, and what do you ask her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any hours I could, make food, serve, carry stock, because that's still hands-on. I'd also learn the bakery's ordering system, which has some thinking in it. It's not glamorous, but I know it and the people trust me.

say: I'd say two years is **far too quick** for anyone to prepare.
I'd write to my local councillor so my voice is on record.
think: The exam route feels **pointless** if the job might not exist when I finish.
I'm thin on every side: no savings, a huge loan and a bakery wage that depends on the day.
do: Ask the bakery for **more hours** and learn its ordering and books.
Ask my aunt whether her clients would pay for a **human check**.
feel: **Scared and grim**, like a train ticket when the station closes.
S2.quote: Why pay for qualifications in a job that might not exist by the time I finish?
fieldNote: The exam plan collapses fast and she turns to **hands-on** work she already has.
Looks to her aunt's local, trust-based model as a fallback.
Keeps calm outwardly but her **thin cushion** drives the mood.

steps.text: Stop paying for exam papers immediately
Ask the bakery owner for more hours and learn the ordering
Ask my aunt whether clients would pay for a human check
Write to my local councillor about support for graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a sensible plan, so we should. I'd say it to my housemates, who all tell me I worry too much. I'd mention that some careers are safer than others, and ask them what they'd try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could still get somewhere. If I land a first job in the next year, I'd have four years of experience before the thinking work goes, and that could count for something. I'd have to find a role that survives, maybe advisory or compliance, where a person signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any junior role I could get, even if it's at a payroll bureau on low pay, and ask for exam sponsorship in the first month. I'd save fifty pounds a month. I'd also pick up one or two of the AI tools properly, so I'm someone who can supervise them. And I'd keep my bakery hours for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful in a measured way, and anxious about the first job. If I get that first one, I think I can move. The five years make it feel like a puzzle and not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build one proper step, a job, a qualification and some savings, before things change. Two years lets me do only one of those, if I'm lucky. It's the difference between climbing a ladder and jumping off a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the next student about to choose accounting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say still do it if you love the work, but pick a firm that trains people, and learn the tools from day one. I'd say avoid taking on big loans if possible. And I'd tell them not to wait until graduation to look for experience.

I'd ask my housemates what they'd try.
think: A first job soon would give me **four years of experience** before the thinking work goes.
I'd need a role that survives, such as advisory or compliance, where a person signs off.

feel: **Measured hope**, anxious about the first job, with a puzzle instead of a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years lets me build one proper step, a job, a qualification and some savings, before things change.
fieldNote: She treats five years as time to build one **step at a time**.

steps.text: Take any junior payroll or practice role within the first year
Ask the new employer for exam sponsorship
Learn two AI tools well enough to supervise them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is more than enough for people to adjust. I'd say not to panic, and I'd tell my aunt that her bureau should plan for it. I'd probably be the one in the family who explains it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel that I can build a proper career. I'd have time to pass the exams, work three or four years in a firm and move into advisory work. The loan would be paid off sooner than now. I just have to get that first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending applications and, once hired, work through the full set of exams. I'd save a hundred pounds a month, pay down the loan and maybe rent a small flat on my own by year four. I'd use AI tools more as they become normal at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough, though I'm still carrying the same loan and the same gap on my CV. I'd feel I have time, which is a luxury. It's nice not to feel the walls close in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what do you picture at thirty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By thirty-three I'd like to be a qualified accountant in a small practice, perhaps working with my aunt's clients. I'd have my own flat and a cat. Nothing grand, but a life I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do differently now because of the longer time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study the exams with more patience and choose a firm that has a training plan, not just the biggest name. I'd also try to build local contacts, because small firms hire people they know. And I'd take the bakery job less personally.

say: I'd say ten years is **more than enough** to adjust, so people shouldn't panic.
I'd tell my aunt her bureau should plan for it.
think: I could build a **proper career**: exams, three or four years in a firm, then advisory work.
I just need that first job.

Save a hundred pounds a month and pay down the loan.

fieldNote: A decade makes her usual **step-by-step** plan realistic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because the exam plan falls apart and I have almost no cushion. What would help is employers who sponsor exams, a pause on loan payments and honest guidance on which roles last. Local contacts would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that people who are steady aren't fine just because they look it. I'm calm in public, but I count every pound. I'd like employers to know that a pass degree and a bakery job is not the same as not trying.

headlineQuote: A pass degree and a bakery job is not the same as not trying.
portrait: Beth (23) rents a room in a shared house in **Lakeside**, owes a large loan and has about ten days of savings.
She holds a pass in accounting and finance with no internship and has had four interviews from seventy applications.
She is organised and **list-driven**, and uses AI tools now and then to practise exam questions.
She works part-time at a bakery and aims for payroll, small practices and **accountancy exams**.
She stays measured in public, but with two years' warning her exam plan collapses.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because her exam plan falls apart and she has no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Employers who **sponsor exams**, a loan pause and honest guidance on which roles last.
